title: Ecologically Derived Suicidal Ideation in Adolescents: Proximal Associations with Self-Referential Thoughts.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Suicide is the second leading cause of death among 10-14 and 25-34-year-olds in the U.S. Suicidal ideation (SI) is one of the strongest predictors of death by suicide in children and adolescents. There is a critical need for identifying time-variant short-term risk factors for suicidal ideation. Although trait self-criticism (i.e. thinking focused on negative self-evaluation) and self-reassurance (i.e. providing self-compassion) are known vulnerabilities for SI, their short-term, real-time association with SI remains remarkably understudied. To address this critical gap, we examined how self-critical and self-reassuring responses may affect in-the-moment and subsequent SI in a youth's environment.
METHOD: Levels of self-criticism, self-reassurance, and SI were assessed 3 times per day over 2 weeks using ecological momentary assessment (EMA) technology in 114 12- to 15-year-old youth recruited primarily from child psychiatric hospital programs in the Northeast of the U.S. Participants were asked to rate how self-critical and self-reassuring they had been since the last prompt.
RESULTS: A series of zero-inflated negative binomial mixed models showed that greater levels of self-criticism compared to one's own average levels beyond the overall sample's average were linked to higher SI in both the current and the next assessment window. Lower between but not within-person self-reassurance was linked to higher SI.
CONCLUSIONS: The findings highlight the need for further research on the clinical relevance of assessing and targeting self-criticism and enhancing self-reassurance in the day-to-day lives of youth to reduce SI.

journal.name: JOURNAL OF CLINICAL CHILD AND ADOLESCENT PSYCHOLOGY
